beats.act: cold open
beats.narration_text: Shalom — this is Liam, in for Divyank. Ask which API technology is 'better' — FastAPI or gRPC — and you're already asking the wrong question. Real systems run both, on purpose, for completely different reasons. Let's take apart what each one actually is, and why neither one replaces the other.

beats.act: Act I — Two Answers to One Question
beats.narration_text: R-P-C means remote procedure call — making a function run on another machine feel like calling it locally. Both FastAPI and gRPC solve that exact same old problem. They just answer it completely differently.

beats.act: Act I — Two Answers to One Question
beats.narration_text: FastAPI: a Python web framework, built on Starlette and Pydantic, speaking HTTP and JSON. gRPC: Google's own framework, built directly on HTTP slash 2 and Protocol Buffers — a binary format, not text.

beats.act: Act I — Two Answers to One Question
beats.narration_text: Two formats, two commitments. JSON: readable in a browser, debuggable with curl, loosely typed at the wire level. Protocol Buffers: a strict schema file, compiled into code, every field typed before a single byte is ever sent.

beats.act: Act I — Two Answers to One Question
beats.narration_text: A JSON payload is a postcard — open it, read it, anyone can. That's not a weakness. For a public, human-facing API, it's the entire point.

beats.narration_text: Pick HTTP 1.1 with JSON, or HTTP 2 with protobuf. One request per connection versus many multiplexed streams on a single connection. Readable text versus a compact binary wire format compiled straight from a schema.

beats.act: Act II — Why You'd Run Both
beats.narration_text: Somebody has to stand between a browser that only speaks JSON and a fleet of internal services that only speak protobuf. That's a real job, with a real name — the gateway.

beats.act: Act II — Why You'd Run Both
beats.narration_text: The actual pattern, in production, constantly: FastAPI faces the public internet — browsers, mobile apps, third-party integrations. Behind it, internal services talk to each other over gRPC. FastAPI translates one request into the other.

beats.act: Act III — What Each One Is Actually For
beats.narration_text: A battery-powered device, reporting sensor readings over a constrained connection, cannot afford to repeat a JSON object's field names on every single message. Every byte is a cost it actually pays.

beats.act: Act III — What Each One Is Actually For
beats.narration_text: FastAPI's real strengths: automatic interactive documentation, generated straight from the code. Native readability for debugging. Instant compatibility with every browser and HTTP client that has ever existed.

Native readability for debugging
Instant compatibility, every HTTP client

beats.act: Act III — What Each One Is Actually For
beats.narration_text: gRPC's real strengths: payloads a fraction of the size of the equivalent JSON. A persistent HTTP slash 2 connection, avoiding a fresh handshake per call. Four interaction patterns built in, not bolted on — including true bidirectional streaming.

show.event: three chips snap in

items: A fraction of JSON's payload size

Four patterns built in — including bidirectional streaming
props.caption: services that never stop talking

beats.act: Act III — What Each One Is Actually For
beats.narration_text: That's exactly why gRPC shows up in I-O-T and mobile: constrained bandwidth, constrained battery, and a connection that has to stay open and cheap, not reopen every single time.

beats.act: Act III — What Each One Is Actually For
beats.narration_text: Streaming is the one capability REST never had natively. A sensor can keep a single gRPC connection open and push readings continuously — no polling, no reconnecting, just one open channel doing real work.

beats.act: Act IV — The Tradeoffs Nobody Mentions
beats.narration_text: A sealed protocol is fast precisely because it refuses to be read by just anyone. That's gRPC's real cost, and it's worth saying out loud.

shot.prompt: real archival wax-seal photo -- illustrative of a sealed, binary protocol, not a literal depiction. Already sourced, see media/A4-1.source.txt

beats.act: Act IV — The Tradeoffs Nobody Mentions
beats.narration_text: A browser cannot speak gRPC directly — its networking APIs can't read the HTTP slash 2 trailers the protocol depends on. Reaching gRPC from a browser needs gRPC-Web and a proxy translating in between, every single time.

gRPC-Web + a proxy, every time

beats.act: Act IV — The Tradeoffs Nobody Mentions
beats.narration_text: Debug a failing FastAPI call: open dev tools, read the JSON, done. Debug a failing gRPC call: decode a binary payload against a dot-proto schema, or reach for a specialized tool built for exactly that job.

beats.act: verdict
beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. FastAPI and gRPC solve the same old problem — making a remote call feel local — with opposite commitments: HTTP and JSON, readable and loosely typed, versus HTTP two and Protocol Buffers, compact and strictly schemaed. Running both isn't redundancy — it's a gateway pattern: FastAPI faces browsers and third parties, gRPC connects internal services, and each side gets the contract it actually needs. Each one's real strength shows up in its use case: FastAPI's readability and universal compatibility for anyone asking a question, gRPC's compact streaming connections for services — and devices, like I-O-T sensors — that never stop talking to each other. And the honest tradeoff cuts both ways: the format that's easy to inspect is expensive to move at scale, and the format that's cheap to move is hostile to a browser, or a curious human, on the other end.
